title: Clinical Mastery: Cavernous Sinus Thrombosis (CST)
summary: Cavernous Sinus Thrombosis (CST) is a life-threatening, septic or aseptic thrombosis of the cavernous sinus, representing a true neuro-ophthalmologic emergency. Rapid recognition of the hallmark 'ophthalmoplegia with proptosis' is critical to mitigating high morbidity and mortality.

sections.title: 1. Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: CST is the formation of a clot within the cavernous sinus, a paired dural venous sinus receiving drainage from the ophthalmic veins, superficial cortical veins, and pterygoid plexus. Pathophysiology involves hematogenous spread of infection (often from the 'danger triangle' of the face) leading to endophlebitis, thrombosis, and subsequent venous congestion.

sections.title: 3. Red Flags (Medical Emergency)
content: Rapid onset of bilateral orbital signs
Decreased level of consciousness/Meningeal signs
CN III, IV, V1, V2, and VI involvement
Systemic sepsis or hemodynamic instability
Cavernous sinus involvement starting from a dental source

sections.title: 5. Ocular Examination Findings
content: Chemosis: Often severe and aggressive
Proptosis: Typically axial, may become bilateral
Ophthalmoplegia: Complete (Total) usually by early stage
Pupillary changes: Dilated or sluggish due to CN III palsy
Sensory loss: V1/V2 distribution (corneal anesthesia)

content.explanation: Ophthalmoplegia (Total), Trigeminal (V1/V2) pain, Orbital congestion (chemosis/proptosis), Systemic symptoms (fever/sepsis), Imaging (Filling defect), Sepsis (Staph aureus source)

sections.title: 7. Diagnostic Workup Protocol
content: Step 1: Blood cultures (aerobic/anaerobic) and complete metabolic panel.
Step 2: Urgent Contrast-enhanced MRI/MRV of brain and orbits (Gold Standard).
Step 3: If MRI contraindicated, CT scan with venography.
Step 4: Lumbar puncture if meningitis suspected after stabilization.
Step 5: Emergent ENT consultation for primary source drainage.

rows: No chemosis/bilateral signs; optic nerve involvement early

sections.title: 9. Management & Treatment Strategy
content: Antibiotics: High-dose IV antibiotics (Vancomycin + Ceftriaxone + Metronidazole) covering MRSA and anaerobes.
Surgical: Drainage of primary site (e.g., sphenoid sinusotomy) is mandatory.
Anticoagulation: Controversy exists; reserved for cases of worsening neurological status or thrombus extension.
Steroids: High-dose IV dexamethasone to reduce inflammation/cranial nerve compression.

sections.title: 10. Key Clinical Pearls
content: CST is the only condition where orbital congestion rapidly spreads from one eye to the other via the intercavernous sinuses.
Always evaluate corneal sensitivity early; loss indicates significant V1 involvement.
Prognosis: Mortality has dropped from 80% to 20% with modern antibiotics and neuro-imaging.
Don't forget the 'Danger Triangle'—superficial facial infections can track posteriorly via the facial vein to the cavernous sinus.
